title: the Bhagavata's tenth book continued
hook: a poor man visits his richest friend, forgets to ask for anything, and walks home happy anyway
carry: a handful of rice, eaten with delight

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Bhagavata's tenth book continued with the Syamantaka jewel: a rumor, a trail into the forest, and the truth told in public: he gives the jewel back. Did you check something before repeating it? Day nine hundred eighty-six.
screen: `THE TENTH BOOK, CONTINUED.` · `HE GIVES THE JEWEL BACK.`

segments.voice: A thin man in a torn cloth is standing at the gates of Dwaraka, holding a small bundle. He's a brahmin, poor enough that his family often goes hungry. His wife has sent him. Go to your old friend, she said. The one you studied with as a boy. He's the lord of Dwaraka now. Surely he'll help. The man didn't want to ask. He came mostly to see his friend's face. And in the bundle is the only gift his house could find: a few handfuls of flattened rice, begged from the neighbors. Tradition calls him Sudama.
screen: `A POOR MAN AT THE GATES.` → `GO TO YOUR OLD FRIEND.` → `A BUNDLE OF FLATTENED RICE.`

segments.voice: Krishna sees him from across the palace and gets up from where he's sitting with Rukmini, runs to him, and embraces him. He washes his friend's feet. Rukmini herself fans him. And the two old classmates talk about school, about Sandipani's house, the teacher we met earlier this week. Krishna reminds him of a night when the teacher's wife sent them for firewood, a storm caught them in the forest, and they held hands in the dark until their teacher came looking at dawn and blessed them. Then Krishna asks, smiling: what did you bring me? The brahmin is too ashamed to show it. So Krishna takes the bundle himself, opens it, and eats a handful of the rice with delight. As he reaches for more, Rukmini gently catches his hand, as if to say: that's enough. That one handful is plenty for everything your friend will ever need. The brahmin stays the night, and in the morning he walks home. He never asked. Krishna never offered. And he walks home happy, thinking, in paraphrase: he didn't give me wealth so that I wouldn't become proud and forget him. Then he reaches his village, and can't find his hut. In its place is a house shining like a palace, and his wife comes out to meet him. The Bhagavata gives him a last reflection: Krishna gives a great deal and counts it as little, and takes a small thing from his devotee and counts it as a great deal. The brahmin lives on in that house, and the text says he keeps his heart where it was. On Krishna.
screen: `KRISHNA RUNS TO HIM.` · `THE NIGHT IN THE STORM, AT SCHOOL.` · `ONE HANDFUL IS ENOUGH.` · `HE NEVER ASKED.` · then, large: `GIVES MUCH, COUNTS IT LITTLE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Let your eyes move slowly around the room and rest on one ordinary thing you already have: a cup, a blanket, a window, a pair of shoes. Stay with it. Notice who made it, or gave it, or what it has carried you through. The brahmin walked home glad before he knew what was waiting there. Let some of that gladness rest on this one small thing. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. If you don't, simply let it be enough for now. The bell holds the time.
Sudama, the poor brahmin and Krishna's boyhood friend. Today, his flattened rice, and a friend who counts a small gift as a great one.
Your line: a handful of rice, eaten with delight. Today, when someone gives you something small, count it as large: tell them exactly what it meant. Day nine hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Hindus tell the story of Sudama, also called Kuchela in South India, as a picture of friendship with God, and in some places devotees offer flattened rice to Krishna in memory of it.

fork.setup: you're the poor brahmin. your richest friend has welcomed you like a king. it's morning, and you're leaving. what do you do?
options: say nothing, and walk home glad you saw him.
fork.reveal: he asks for nothing and walks home happy, and finds his hut has become a palace.

trapdoor: what you thought: a poor man visits a rich friend and comes home rich.
what it means: he never asks, and the Bhagavata says Krishna counts a small gift from a devotee as a great one.
what a scholar hears: in these chapters the Bhagavata calls him a brahmin, Krishna's friend; tradition names him Sudama, or Kuchela in the south.

notes: 'Later retellings call him Sudama' / Kuchela: the Bhagavata 10.80–81 does not name him in these chapters as far as this writer knows; confirm before keeping the trapdoor's third floor.
Year 1 day 190 used the flattened rice to illustrate Gita 9.26; this day centers on the walk home and the brahmin's reflection instead.
Rukmini stopping Krishna's hand after the first handful, and the 'gives much, counts it little' reflection: confirm verses (10.81.10–11, 10.81.35 or nearby).
Offering flattened rice (aval/poha) to Krishna in memory of the story (e.g. Kuchela Dinam at Guruvayur) is a regional custom; confirm wording in howItsDone.
Not a week end (987 is); 987 is the next run, 'kirtan repertoire'.
Index word is the truncated 'the Bhagavata's tenth book continued'; kept exactly.

Editor pass: 'borrowed' changed to 'begged' (the text has him beg the rice); 'later retellings call him Sudama' reframed as 'tradition calls him', since it is a claim about other texts; cut the stock 'here's the part worth staying with'; practice (open palms holding a small gift) and carry (give one small thing) repeated day 974's tray and carry and day 968's open palms, so the practice now rests on gratitude for one ordinary thing and the carry asks the listener to count a small gift as large, as Krishna does in 10.81; 'many' dropped from howItsDone.
